name: Pebble (CockroachDB storage engine)
workload: 6 standard YCSB workloads (A-F: mixes of reads/updates/inserts/scans, zipf key distribution) run both at the CockroachDB level and directly on the storage engine, with datasets sized to fit in memory (plus separate out-of-cache testing mentioned but not detailed).
claimed_speedup: "Pebble meets or exceeds RocksDB on the 6 standard YCSB workloads"; largest margin on workload C (100% reads), attributed to better concurrency in Pebble's block/table cache structures. No exact percentages given in text, only charts.
hardware: Not specified (blog states testing was run on AWS/GCP but gives no CPU model, instance type, or flags)
stars_or_usage: 6,043 stars; default storage engine of CockroachDB since v20.2 (Nov 2020), used in production at scale
tradeoffs: Go, not a drop-in RocksDB replacement (does not implement column families, transactions, backups, universal/FIFO compaction, plain table format, etc.); README carries an explicit warning that opening a RocksDB DB with unsupported features can silently corrupt data.
caveats: Numbers exist only as charts embedded in the post, not as text; no CPU model, instance type, or compiler/Go-version flags stated, so this falls short of Tier A/B despite being a real, code-backed benchmark (YCSB harness is public in the Pebble repo). CockroachDB-level comparison shows a much smaller gap than the storage-engine-only comparison, since CockroachDB has other bottlenecks.
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia search "pebble rocksdb" -> Cockroach Labs engineering blog post "Pebble: A RocksDB Inspired Key-Value Store Written in Go" (2020-09-15), cross-checked against the pebble GitHub README and nightly-benchmark page (https://cockroachdb.github.io/pebble/, which is Pebble-only historical tracking, not a RocksDB comparison).

name: Badger
workload: WiscKey-style key/value-separated LSM benchmark on an AWS i3.large instance (2 vCPU, 15.25GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD, ~100K random-read IOPS at 4KB via fio): loaded 250M x 128B values (35GB), 75M x 1KB values (73GB), and 5M x 16KB values (76GB), each keyed by 22-byte keys, sized so the dataset does not fit entirely in RAM in either engine; measured data-loading time/output size, random Get, and sorted-range Iterate.
claimed_speedup: Random key lookup (Get) at least 3.5x faster than RocksDB (Badger's LSM tree is small enough to fit in RAM); data loading 4.5x faster at 1KB values and 11.7x faster at 16KB values (0.86x-14x faster overall depending on value size, with small values ~2-3x slower); ~4x faster Get overall and an estimated 86% lower AWS instance cost due to running on cheap NVMe storage instead of large-RAM RocksDB instances. Iterate (range scan) is slower than RocksDB.
hardware: AWS i3.large: 2 vCPU, 15.25GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD
stars_or_usage: 15,773 stars; storage engine of the Dgraph graph database
tradeoffs: Pure Go (no cgo dependency on RocksDB's C++), based on the WiscKey key/value-separation design; slower than RocksDB for sorted range iteration; value-log design means space amplification/GC tuning matters for update-heavy workloads.
caveats: This is dgraph's own first-party benchmark; instance type (AWS i3.large) is stated but the exact CPU model and Go compiler version are not, so it falls short of Tier A. The original open.dgraph.io post is dead; content recovered via Wayback Machine (2017 snapshot). Benchmark harness (dgraph-io/badger-bench) and raw logs are linked from the post as public artifacts. Numbers are from 2017, an early Badger version; current Badger performance characteristics may differ.
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia search "Badger key value store dgraph" -> dgraph engineering blog post "Badger – A fast key-value store written natively in Go" (open.dgraph.io/post/badger/, 2017), recovered via web.archive.org since the original domain no longer serves the post.
